days.reason: This is the central account of the last meal (the Passover meal) where Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper (verses 26-29). The text also describes the preparations for the meal and Jesus' prediction of betrayal, which is the core of Maundy Thursday's liturgy.

The account of the Gethsemane prayer (verses 36-46) is a central part of the narrative for Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. It shows Jesus' human anguish and his complete surrender to the Father's will ('let your will be done'), as well as the disciples' failure to keep watch.
The arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane (verses 47-56) marks the transition from the last meal to the passion narrative. Judas' betrayal and Jesus' calmness in surrendering are central themes for the day.

The first trial before the Sanhedrin (verses 57-68) often takes place in the context of Maundy Thursday or early Good Friday in the liturgy. Here, Jesus is accused of blasphemy and threatening the temple, and he confirms his identity as the Messiah and Son of God.

Peter's three denials (verses 69-75) occur parallel to the trial. This is a central part of the passion narrative often read on Maundy Thursday to emphasize human weakness and the fulfillment of Jesus' prophecies.

The introduction (verses 1-5) sets the scene for Passover and the planning of Jesus' death. Although the main events (the crucifixion) take place on Good Friday, this conspiracy is the direct prerequisite for the day.
Judas' agreement to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (verses 14-16) is a critical link in the passion narrative leading up to the crucifixion on Good Friday.
The trial against Jesus (verses 57-68) is a preparation for the final judgment and execution that takes place on Good Friday. It reveals the charges and the verdict that lead to the crucifixion.
